title: Quantization SLA breakpoints — field notes
body:
Summary:

These are field notes from a set of ad-hoc experiments exploring "tipping points" where quantization choices (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ/FP8) and kernel selection cause sudden jumps in observed SLA violations (tail latency and quality regressions) across two model archetypes: MLP-heavy encoder stacks and attention-dominant decoder stacks. The goal: find actionable breakpoints we can encode into runtime routing policies and docs for SRE/product to avoid surprise regressions during rollouts.

High-level observations (TL;DR):
- There are discrete zones where a single-layer quantization mismatch or kernel pack choice causes >30% increase in 95/99 latency tail for small-batch interactive workloads. Not gradual — a cliff.
- Quality regressions (perplexity / downstream QA F1) often correlate with the same layers that produce latency cliffs, but not always; sometimes numeric instability in AWQ/GPTQ causes quality noise with no latency delta.
- FP8 variants reduce latency tail in high-memory-pressure scenarios (long context) compared to AWQ on some kernels due to reduced kernel fragmentation and fewer slow fallback paths.
- Kernel packing (tile width/height choices) interacts with per-request sequence length distribution — mismatched packing increases memory movement and causes non-linear latency amplification.

Experiment setup and test harness notes:
- Workloads: three synthetic workloads + two replayed production traces (chat-short: 32 tok reqs, chat-long: 512 tok reqs, batch-embed: 512 batch of 64).
- Models: "arch-A" (4B-ish MLP heavy encoder), "arch-B" (7B decoder-style, attention heavy). We used the same validated weights rerun through GPTQ, AWQ, INT8 pack tooling.
- Hardware: A100-40GB, H100-80GB (both baremetal instances). Kernel builds: baseline kernels v1.18 (vector-lane-alloc), patched kernels v1.20 (improved packing and memcpy coalescing).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), CPU/GPU % utilization, GPU DRAM bandwidth, KV cache hit rate, token quality (perplexity), downstream QA accuracy (SQuAD-style), and per-layer quantization error summary (L2 residuals).
- Run harness: 30-minute steady-state runs after 15-minute warmup. For small-batch interactive runs we logged jitter and inter-request gap patterns.

Notable phenomena and examples:
1) Layer-local cliffing (arch-A / AWQ / int8-mapped kernels):
- When we aggressively apply AWQ with per-tile group size 64 -> 32 for the larger MLP matmuls, p95 jumps from 45ms to 78ms for 1-2% of requests. Tracing shows a handful of large matmul ops that fall back to the slow path due to alignment mismatch in the vector-lane scheduler.
- Root cause: kernel schedule tries fast-vector kernel but misses alignment, then runtime picks a generic emulation kernel that has much worse L1 cache behavior.
- Mitigation: add alignment-aware pre-check in kernel-selector, fallback to packed-int8 kernel instead of generic emulation for these cases. Also, conservative group-size for MLP-heavy layers in AWQ.

2) FP8 improves long-context tail at high concurrency (arch-B / FP8 / v1.20 kernels):
- Long context runs (512 tokens) with ~8 concurrent streams showed that FP8 with high packing reduces kernel fragmentation — fewer tiny memcpy ops. The result: p99 down by ~20% and throughput up 12%.
- Tradeoff: slightly higher perplexity variance (+0.5-1.2) depending on layer scaling. Not always acceptable for QA-critical paths.

3) GPTQ numeric noise separate from latency cliffs:
- GPTQ variants sometimes show small downstream QA accuracy drops (1–3%) without any change to runtime latency. Investigation points to grouped quantization scale drifts in attention key/proj layers; quality loss is visible in L2 residual heatmaps but not in memory access patterns.
- Mitigation: tie evaluation regressions to rollout gating (quality gating) independent of latency SLO.

4) Kernel packing vs sequence-length distribution mismatch:
- When the distribution of sequence lengths in a batch has high variance, certain packing strategies that optimize for average length produce excessive copy/transpose overhead for the longer tails. Observed as highly skewed latency per-request within a single batch.
- Practical fix: when variance(seq_len) > threshold, use a dual-path packing that separates long-tail requests into a separate micro-batch. This reduces p99 in interactive settings but lowers aggregate throughput slightly.

Measurements that mattered: what to log and where
- Per-layer op execution time and variance (important to correlate with quality regression hot layers).
- Kernel dispatch decision and actual kernel id used (helps spot selector misfires).
- Memory copy sizes and counts per-request (highly correlated with tail latency).
- Alignment / vector-lane fallback counts (rare events but catastrophic).
- KV cache hit/miss and prefix reuse — small changes in KV warming strategy magnify quantization instability.

Operational recommendations for rollouts
- Don't roll AWQ/GPTQ at full fleet — start canary on dedicated pool with real traffic replay; gate on both (latency tail & quality) using the small set of tests we defined (short chat p99, long chat p99, SQuAD-like eval).
- Add quick safety net to runtime: if per-request kernel-fallback-rate > 0.5% and p99 increases more than X ms over baseline, automatically route new traffic to a conservative (FP8 or int8-packed) profile.
- Add confidence band thresholds for quality: a 1% downstream-accuracy drop should trigger rollback unless expected by product.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- How reproducible are the alignment fallback events across driver/firmware versions? We saw differences between H100 firmware 2.1 and 2.3. Need deeper testing matrix.
- Can we synthesize a cheap, online kernel-health metric from GPU perf counters that predicts fallback before it impacts p99?
- Explore mixed-precision across layers (FP8 for attention, AWQ for MLP) as a routing-time model variant. Build an automated fast-eval for hybrid variants.
- Add script to auto-generate per-layer L2 residual maps and correlate with cache behavior.

Appendix: quick commands / artifacts
- harness: experiments/harness/quant-breakpoint-harness (see GH PR above).
- quick-run for interactive test: run_local --model arch-B --quant awq --kernels v1.18 --trace chat-short --warmup 900 --duration 1800 --log-per-layer
- trace keys to look for: kernel_selected, fallback_count, memcpy_ops, per_layer_exec_ms, perplexity_delta

Notes: This doc is a working artifact. Intend to convert high-confidence mitigations into a rollout playbook and add routing policies into redwood-console as flags. Also need to coordinate with release-engineering before any kernel selector patch lands; small mis-schedule can flip hundreds of hosts into the slow path.

-- Maya
